tip: 'Basta que' (it is enough that) triggers the subjunctive: 'peça', not 'pede'.
'Caso' means if and takes the subjunctive: 'caso precise' = if you need. It is more formal than 'se'.
'Experimentar' means to try or taste something new: 'experimentar a comida' = try the food. Not the same as 'tentar'.
'Convidar' uses 'para' for the event: 'nos convidou para o churrasco' = invited us to the barbecue.
The object pronoun 'os' in 'os encontrou' reads formal; everyday Brazilian speech says 'encontrou eles' instead.
'Lhes' means to them and marks the indirect object: 'lhes explicou' = explained to them.
With 'vou' plus an infinitive, the pronoun sits between them: 'vou te buscar' = I'll pick you up.
'Conhecer' means to meet for the first time: 'nos conheceu na faculdade' = we met in college. Reencounter is 'encontrar'.
'Acho que' takes the indicative, but negating it to 'não acho que' flips the verb to the subjunctive: 'venha'.
'Fazer amizade' means 'to make friends'. Brazilians use many 'fazer' expressions: 'fazer compras' (shop), 'fazer fila' (queue), 'fazer sentido' (make sense).
'É estranho que' takes the subjunctive 'tenha ligado' even though the event is real; the emotion triggers it, not doubt.
'Cuide' is the polite command, borrowed from the subjunctive: 'cuide bem' = take good care. Casual speech says 'cuida'.
'A' = her (formal direct object). 'Não a vi' = I didn't see her. Formal; spoken: 'não vi ela.'
'Lhe' here means 'to you', matching 'você'; it isn't always 'to him'. 'Eu lhe garanto' is 'I assure you'.
'Talvez' triggers the subjunctive, so 'pedir' becomes 'peça', not 'pede'. The mood marks the outcome as uncertain.
In 'olha só', 'só' isn't 'only'; it just adds emphasis, so 'olha só' means 'just look'.
Casual Brazilian commands use the he/she form: 'segura', not the textbook 'segure'.
Negative commands switch to subjunctive endings: 'não jogue'. An a-verb like 'jogar' takes '-e'.
Colloquial 'deixa eu' plus an infinitive means let me: 'deixa eu terminar'. Careful grammar would say 'deixe-me terminar'.
Feelings take the subjunctive after 'que': 'fico feliz que você esteja', not 'está'.
'Tomar cuidado' means be careful, literally take care: 'toma cuidado' is the everyday warning.
'Tomara que' means let's hope and always takes the subjunctive: 'tomara que dê', from the verb 'dar'.
For a future when, use the future subjunctive: 'quando chegar' means when you arrive, not 'quando chega'.
Formal commands use the subjunctive form: 'confirme'. The informal version to a friend would be 'confirma'.
After a place word, 'mesmo' means right or exactly: 'aqui mesmo' means right here.
'A gente' means we or us in casual speech: 'pra gente' means for us here.
The conditional (would) adds its ending to the whole infinitive: 'cozinhar' plus 'íamos' gives 'cozinharíamos'.
'A menos que' means unless and always takes the subjunctive: 'a menos que você estude', not 'estuda'.
'Oxalá' means hopefully, from Arabic, and forces the subjunctive: 'oxalá eu passe', not 'passo'.
'Puxar' means to pull, not to push: 'puxa a porta'. The push sign says 'empurre'.
